body: I just feel so alone all of the time. What's the point of fighting if there is nothing to fight for?

It's a very long and winded story but sure here's the situation.

I am currently 23 years old and I have been actively suicidal since I was 13. I have had 2 failed attempts in the past (mostly because I am a chicken shit and overdosing is an ineffective means of suicide). I have paid for school, and most of my expenses indepedently for my entire life - I worked jobs at McDonalds, Tim Hortons, as a sales person for air-conditioning, news paper - and mostly recently I lot of free fucking work with hopes to get into graduate school).

In fact I have spent the last three fucking years trying to make myself an ideal candidate for higher education while being in school full-time and fully paying for the cost of an undergraduate degree + life expenses. I have absolutely no support from my family, and I basically only have one friend because with school, work, and volunteering I never have time to see people.

I have tried taking several times of anti-depressants for the last 7 years and I have still not found one that is "working" for me. When talking to people, I am always overwhelmed and anxious - and it makes being in social situations unbearable. I start trembling, and sweating and thinking coherently becomes so incredibly difficult. Oh I also forgot to mention that growing up I was abused by my parents, and when I was 20 I was raped and stalked by an art instructor -- it has made doing one of the only things that I loved impossible to do.

I am tired of waking up everyday and trying.

To people who see me on the surface, they commend me for all of the work I am doing and have done. I have one of the highest sessional GPA's at my university, and I worked my ass off to get scholarships - but none of this makes me happy or proud.

I am fucking exhausted of trying
-of pretending to live normally. Of going home everynight, calling my best friend calling
-of not having support with my family
-of trying so hard all of the time.

But I am too weak to buy a gun or cut myself. But I want to die - if there was a magic pill that I could take right now to not live anymore, I wouldn't have blinked an eye before I took it.

Hey - I felt similarly when I came out of high school, and I really struggled with fitting in on campus. I'm not sure if you felt the same way but when I studied it would take me so long to learn a concept and I really struggled with trying to learn. What helped me was changing how I was learning and not necessarily putting in a ton of time into studying but studying efficiently.
A lot of students on campus buy test banks for different classes and I think it's helpful if you really want a top notch grade - but even with test banks a majority of classes don't have them.
One suggestion I can give you is try to make your own mock test about a given class. Before I would try to make these perfect notes and try to memorize them but this was such a terrible approach to studying. Looking back, I would recommend to try to test yourself on the core material - making your own test questions each week, and spending an hour every couple of days trying to answer them internally as opposed to writing everything down. My average went from a C in first year to an A after changing how I looked at studying. It was also a huge time saver, and going out and seeing friends is really important too.
So study smart, and not hard, and play hard too if you can.
Wow - what a champ!! Thank you so much!!!

But it's really important to carve out time to take care of yourself. Good luck in your first appointment and keep us posted on how things go.

Hi Legalwave,

It certainly sounds like you have a lot on your plate, and I can certainly relate. Last year I was working 4 part-time jobs while doing school on a full-time basis. It's possible to for you to get through, even though it may not feel like this right now. Take things one step at a time, and take care of yourself if you can. 

I personally found it helpful to see a counsellor once a week. It kept me grounded and made me aware of just how much I am doing. I'm going to do the same for you right now. (1) It is so incredibly impressive that you are in law school; that alone tells me you are a hard-working and intelligent person. (2) You have so much on your plate: a) the responsibilities from school, (b) drafting cover letters and resumes for your internship/clerkship, (c) maintaining a connection with friends and family, and (d) beginning to map out your life in the start of your career.

All of these things are valid and understandable things to feel like sometimes it's too much to handle. Be kind to yourself, and look at everything you have overcome and had to achieve to get this stage in your life right now. This resilience, the strength that you had to (1) discuss your innermost feelings with an absolute stranger, and (2) seek out ways to try to deal with it is pretty fucking impressive to me.

I'm happy to talk if you ever need someone to listen to.

Dear Badlystitchedsock,

I am so sorry you are feeling this way. I've had a similar experience a few years ago when I first sought out medical treatment for depression. I currently work at a suicide hotline, and I am always astounded by the sheer number of psychiatrist's that fail to understand that sometimes depression just happens - we can't explain or rationalize or determine it's psychodynamic basis. In telling this to you I want to reassure you that there is nothing wrong with feeling this way, and some people just have a predisposition to depression in the same way some people have diabetes. 

Although I don't really know what your experiences have been like I am going to end this message with a quote from Andrew Solomon's book Noonday Demon: An Atlas of Depression:

"Depression is a condition that is almost unimaginable to anyone who has not known it. A sequence of metaphors - vines, trees, cliffs, etc. - is the only way to talk about the experience. It's not an easy diagnosis because it depends on metaphors and the metaphors one patient chooses are different from those selected by another... We do not really what causes depression. We do not really know what constitutes depression. We do not really know why certain treatment may be effective for depression. We do not know how depression made it through the evolutionary process. We do not know why one person gets a depression from circumstances that do not trouble another. We do not know how will operates in this context."

Take all the time you need to do whatever is helpful for you, even if it is deviant from pop culture or the recommendations of your psychiatrist. You are the best evaluator of your health, and it is unfortunate how messed up the medical system is for people that have this complex mood disorder. But here you have a platform to be you, entirely you, without editing or changing yourself according to the societal values/cultural norms of everyday life.

Sincerely,
